name: Regression toward the mean (height)

lead: Regression toward the mean describes how the children of unusually tall or short parents tend, on average, to be closer to the population average than their parents were. Paediatric endocrinologists pair it with the mid-parental height, a figure derived from both parents' heights, to give a target range for a growing child.

For people who want to understand their own height ceiling, it is the usual starting point for setting expectations before adding other information such as growth charts and bone age. Clinical reviews treat parental height as one of the standard predictors of growth outcomes, including how children respond to growth hormone therapy.

paras: Practitioners compare a child's measured height with the range predicted from the parents' heights and look at whether the child sits well above or below it. Forum users on height threads often quote their parents' heights alongside their own to estimate a potential. Doctors combine the figure with growth velocity and bone age.

The estimate is an average for a population, so individuals can fall well above or below it. In clinical practice, a child far outside their mid-parental range is typically referred for endocrine assessment, since some hormonal and genetic conditions change growth.

angle.text: The framework gives a baseline for adult height before any intervention. People use it to see whether their own growth is tracking their genetic target and to decide whether a doctor's assessment of growth is worthwhile.

lead: Regression toward the mean is the statistical tendency for offspring of parents with extreme heights to be closer to the average than their parents. Height is strongly heritable, with twin studies cited at roughly 60 to 80 percent, but because many genes and environmental factors contribute, very tall or very short parents typically have children who are tall or short, yet less extreme.[1]

Clinicians use the idea through the mid-parental height, the parents' heights combined into one target value. Paediatric reviews describe predicting expected growth from mid-parental height as essential in monitoring a child's growth.[2] Within looksmaxxing, the concept is used to estimate how tall someone might become and to judge whether growth is on track.

Mid-parental height also appears in clinical definitions. Gigantism is defined by height more than two standard deviations above the mean, or more than two standard deviations above the calculated mid-parental height, prompting hormone work-up.[3] It also features in studies of what predicts response to growth hormone treatment.[4]

paras: A child's height is influenced by inherited variants at hundreds of loci together with nutrition, health and other environmental factors, so a parent-to-child prediction is an average rather than a guarantee.[1] Offspring of extreme parents are expected to be extreme, but less so; that shrinkage toward the population average is the regression effect.[1]

The mid-parental height is the combined figure from both parents, adjusted for the child's sex. A child's final height is usually compared with a range around that target rather than a single number.[2]
Reviews of neonatal and postnatal growth state that expected growth should be predicted from mid-parental height, a step that is frequently omitted.[2]

In growth disorders, the target is a reference point. Gigantism is defined partly as height more than two standard deviations above mid-parental height, which leads to checks for excess growth hormone and related conditions.[3] In Klinefelter syndrome, adult height tends to exceed mid-parental height.[5] In short stature therapy, mid-parental height is one factor shaping how a child responds to growth hormone, alongside age at start and bone age.[4]

Height threads on looksmax.org frequently include parents' heights when users ask about their potential, and the target figure is used as a rough projection. Some users compare it with their actual growth to decide whether to see an endocrinologist.

Published reviews describe mid-parental height as a standard predictor in growth monitoring and treatment response.[2][4] Studies of specific conditions report how final height compares with the parental target, for example in Klinefelter syndrome.[5] These are paediatric reviews rather than trials of the concept itself.
